Zahirul Hoque Khan ----- Petitioner
vs.
Aktaruzzaman Chowdhury & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Mahmudul Amin Choudhury J: This Rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and opposite party No.1 to show cause why the order dated 18-9-96 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Sessions Case No.137 of 1994 arising out of GR Case No.1659 of 1993 of the Court of the learned Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka should not be set aside. 

 2. The short fact leading to this Rule is that, the petitioner as informant lodged the FIR with Tejgaon Police Station, Dhaka alleging that his son-in-law late Humayun Zahir when he was standing in front of his house on 8-9-93 was shot and on hearing alarm and the sound of gun shots local people came and managed to apprehend two of the miscreants with fire-arms. But one of them managed to release himself and fled away. The apprehended miscreant identified himself to be Fazlur Rahman alias Tonmoy who made a confessional statement in committing the murder of said Humayun Zahir. Police on receipt of the FIR took up investigation of the case and got the statement of apprehended accused Fazlur Rahman alias Tonmoy recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by a competent Magistrate and taking the clue from this police arrested on Abdul Matin who also made a confessional statement which was duly recorded by the Magistrate. Then after completion of investigation police submitted charge-sheet against opposite party No.1 and others and the case is now pending before the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka. 

 3. It is the case of the prosecution that on 18-9-96 the learned Additional Sessions Judge took up the examination of PW 25 who is one of the Investigating Officers. The informant raised objection on the ground that in this case there are about 64 witnesses to be examined and before the examination of other witnesses it is not fair and proper to examine Investigating Officers as this may prejudice either side. This was, it appears, opposed both by the defence and also by the prosecutor and the learned Additional Sessions Judge held that the Public Prosecutor has the right to produce witnesses according to the serial prepared by him and the Court cannot ask for changing the serial and it was also held that there was a direction from the High Court Division to dispose of the case with utmost expedition giving priority over all other cases. The trial Court with that observation rejected the informant's prayer for examining the Investigating Officer after examination of the other local witnesses. 

 5. Mr. Muhammad Jamiruddin Sircar, the learned Counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that if before the examination of other local witnesses the Investigating Officers are examined this will cause prejudice to the prosecution and the learned Public Prosecutor was wrong in submitting that he may produce any witness at any time. He further submits that the trial Court also misinterpreted the direction earlier given by a Division Bench of this Court for the speedy disposal of this case. He submits that the High Court Division only directed for expeditious disposal of the case giving priority to this case over all other cases which does not mean that without examining other witnesses the prosecution should close the case. 

 6. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite party No.1, submits that they have no objection if the Rule is made absolute. But they want that the original case should be disposed of expeditiously as earlier ordered by a Division Bench of this Court. 

 7. We have gone through the available materials, particularly order dated 18-9-96 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge and also heard the learned Advocates of both the sides. It appears that in this case 64 witnesses have been cited in the charge-sheet which included two Investigating Officers and the Doctor. It further appears that before 18-9-96 twenty-four local witnesses have been examined and then without exhausting the procedures for securing attendance of the rest of the witnesses the prosecution started examining PW 25 who is one of the Investigating Officers to which the informant raised objection on 18-9-96. Their case is that before concluding the examination of the Investigating officers other local witnesses ought to have been examined as in case of any dispute over place of occurrence contradiction or omission if the Investigating Officer was not made available after his examination the defence will have some advantage and the prosecution will be highly prejudiced. But it appears that the learned Additional Sessions Judge after writing quite a lengthy order rejected the informant's plea on the ground that the Public Prosecutor has the right to produce his witnesses at any time as he desires according to the serial of witnesses prepared by him. He cannot be dictated by the informant or by any other authority. It further appears that the trial Court also held that a Division Bench of this Court in Criminal Miscellaneous Case No.3584/96 directed for expeditious disposal of the case giving priority over all other cases. It has also been held by the learned Additional Sessions Judge that it is the jurisdiction of the Public Prosecutor to produce any witness at any time and this cannot be challenged by any private prosecutor. His duty is only to assist the Public Prosecutor engaged by the State. 

 8. We have considered the submissions made by the learned Advocates of both the sides and also gone through the impugned order. Mr. Khan Saifur Rahman conceding the submission made by Mr. Muhammad Jamiruddin only submits that there should be direction as has been earlier done. He submits that the prosecution in this case has failed to produce witnesses in time so that the trial Court may dispose of the case expeditiously. So, further direction may be given to the trial Court for expeditious disposal of the case. 

 9. As regards the contention that the Public Prosecutor has the right to prepare the serial of the witnesses to be examined there is no doubt about it. Considering the nature of the case and the evidence to be adduced he is to produce the witnesses. It is also a fact that the Public Prosecutor is not bound to examine all the cited witnesses. He may examine any of the witnesses or cite fresh witnesses in support of the prosecution and there is no dispute over that. But the Prosecutor or the prosecution is bound to produce all the cited prosecution witnesses before the Court which is necessary for avoiding adverse opinion against the prosecution as contemplated under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. The Prosecutor may not examine them but he must produce them before the Court. The non-production of the witnesses will definitely go against the prosecution. The Public Prosecutor must remember this. Here it appears that the Public Prosecutor started examining the police witnesses without understanding that if after examination of the remaining local witnesses it transpires that the Investigating Officer shall have to be confronted on omission or contradiction or on the place of occurrence then what will happen to the prosecution ? This will go definitely against the prosecution. For avoiding this situation the Investigating Officers should be examined after the examination of other local witnesses. It is not the case here before us that the informant himself is the Investigating Officer and in such cases the informant and the Investigating Officer is examined twice. Here as the Investigating Officer is not the informant he ought to have been examined after production and examination of the remaining local witnesses. What the Public Prosecutor has done to which the trial Court consented is an act which for ends of justice cannot be accepted and supported. It is not the case of the prosecution that remaining 42 witnesses are all dead or not available in this country. No such report is available before us now and that without issuance of witness warrant for producing or for securing the attendance of the witnesses how and why the Investigating Officer should be examined as has been done in the present case? The ground shown by the trial Court that there was a direction for expeditious disposal of the case does not mean that without complying with the formalities for securing the attendance of the witnesses the case should be disposed of. The spirit of the order is that this case should be disposed of by giving priority over all other cases. This does not mean that without examining other witnesses the prosecution should close the case. Furthermore, it appears that PW 25 is a police official and there is also another Investigating Officer who are not local witnesses and it further appears that PW 25 is serving in the Dhaka Metropolitan Police and, as such, there is no earthly reason for the prosecution and the Court to examine PW 25 before examining the other local witnesses. This situation is not approved by this Court. Mere filing of Hazira of this witness should not be criteria to examine him before examining the other witnesses. The Court and the Prosecutor should not keep any loopholes in the case whose advantage may be taken by the other side. The Prosecutor is not appointed to give any advantage to the defence and so is the trial Court. But it appears that without understanding the implication the Public Prosecutor engaged in this case started examining PW 25 and the Court passed the impugned order which requires our interference. 

 10. As the opposite party No.1 who has entered appearance has conceded that the Rule may be made absolute and a very strong case has been made out by the petitioner, we are inclined to make the Rule absolute and direct the trial Court to remain vigilant so that neither partiy in the case may suffer or cause prejudice to any of the parties. The Prosecutor should take effective steps for production of the remaining public witnesses on the dates fixed by the trial Court and the trial Court should also look into the matter so that police help may be sought in the production of the witnesses. Mere issuance of witness warrant is not sufficient. In such cases something more shall have to be done which is required for ends of justice. In the trial of such cases not only the accused persons want justice but the deceased also wants justice. This should not be lost sight of by the trial Court. 

 12. The order dated 18-9-96 passed by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Sessions Case No.137 of 1994 is hereby set aside and the trial Court is directed to dispose of the case expeditiously in the light of the observation made above. The Prosecutor also should take note of our observation while dealing with this case.
